nigada
(‘that which is uttered loudly’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedic mantras used in yāgas or sacrifices are of four types: ṛk, yajus, सामन् and निगद.
The ṛks are metrical compositions. The yajus are complete sentences in prose. The sāmans are set to मुसिच् and sung.
The nigadas—also called ‘praiṣas’—are words addressed by one priest (generally the अध्वर्यु) to another, loudly, calling on the latter to do a certain thing. For example: ‘prokṣaṇīr āsādaya,’ ‘Approach the vessel containing the holy waters.’
They are, in one sense, yajus, but distinguished from them; since they are uttered loudly whereas the yajus mantras are recited softly.

nigrahasthāna
(‘ground of defeat’)
------------------------------------------
It means a ground of defeat in a debate. The two primary grounds of such a defeat are: misunderstanding or wrong understanding; want of understanding.
If any party in a debate fails to understand or misunderstands his own or the other party’s statement, as also its implication, he is brought to the point at which he has to admit defeat. Shifting of the original proposition or the use of fallacious arguments can lead to defeat.

nigama
(‘that by which [truth is known] clearly’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘nigama’ has been used in several senses in the Hindu scriptures. Since the highest Truth is known or understood properly (‘nitarāṁ gacchanti anena’) through the वेदस्, they are known as ‘Nigama’. So also are the sentences of command contained in them.
A definite conclusion established after countering all objections is also called ‘nigama’ or ‘nigamana’ in the science of लोगिच्, which is also, sometimes, named ‘nigama’.
In a more technical sense, the word ‘āgama’ is used for those tāntrik works where सदाशिव teaches देवी and the word ‘nigama’ for the works wherein the देवी teaches सदाशिव.

nigamana
(‘final conclusion’)
------------------------------------------
The theory of knowledge developed in the न्याय दर्शन or the न्याय philosophy has contributed considerably to Hindu systems of लोगिच्.
While dealing with अनुमान or inference, the second of the four प्रमाणस् accepted by it, the न्याय philosophy puts forward a five membered syllogism of which निगमन is the fifth. They are: प्रतिज्ञा (first proposition asserting something); हेतु(reason); udāharaṇa(example); upanaya (application of the universal to the particular case); निगमन (final conclusion, reasserting the first proposition).
This can be made clear from the following illustration :
Devadatta is a mortal. (pratijñā)
Because he is a human being. (hetu)
All human beings are mortal. For e.g., अशोक, श्रीहर्ष, कालिदास, Tukāram and so on. (udāharaṇa)
Devadatta is also a human being. (upanaya)
Therefore he is mortal. (nigamana)
